topics.title: What Syntelab Creative is
body: Syntelab Creative is one program made of apps. Each app does one kind of work:

points: PDF Organizer reads, arranges, edits and signs PDF documents.
Scribe is a text editor with tools that clean, sort, compare and transform text.
Units converts between units: length, temperature, currencies and many more.
Dev gathers tools for developers: encode and decode, format and check, turn one form of data into another.

body: Each app opens in a window of its own, with its own button on the taskbar, and the apps share one set of settings and one way of working, so what you learn in one is the same in the next.

body.note: Everything happens on your computer. Your documents are never sent anywhere, and nothing about you or your work is collected.

topics.title: The window

points: The bar on top: the Syntelab logo lists the apps (choosing this window's app brings its first page back), and Settings is the gear on the right. The news of the program, Feedback and Support are the small icons at the bottom of the list of tools.
File → Go to Start goes to the first page of the app, and File → Open Settings (Ctrl+,) opens Settings at that app's own part; the other parts are a click away there.
The tabs at the top: every document, binder or tool you open has a tab of its own. A dot on a tab says it has changes that are not saved.
The menus of the app, under the tabs: as a menu bar, as a ribbon or as a panel on the side, whichever you chose.
The rest of the window is the tab in front.

body: Closing a tab that has unsaved changes asks first; so does closing the program.

topics.title: The apps and their windows
body: Click the Syntelab logo at the top of the side bar to see the apps. Click one to open it in its own window; if it is already open, its window comes to the front, so an app never has two windows. The search at the top of the list finds apps, tools and commands.
The apps can be shown as cards, as icons with names or as icons only, and dragged into the order you like. With the keyboard: Alt and the arrow keys. "Reset to default" puts them back.

Each app also has its own shortcut in the Start menu of Windows, in the "Syntelab Creative" folder, and its window can be pinned to the taskbar like any program. Started without an app, the program opens the app you used last.

topics.title: Opening files

points: From an app: File → Open, or Ctrl+O.
By dropping files from a folder onto the window.
From the file manager of your system: double-click a file the program is set to open. In Windows Explorer there is also the right-click menu (see "The right-click menu of Windows Explorer").

body: The program runs as one copy. A file opened from the file manager opens as a new tab in the window of the app that takes it (a PDF in PDF Organizer), which comes to the front.

topics.title: Layout: menu bar, ribbon or side panel
body: The commands of an app can be shown in three ways. They are the same commands; only where they are differs.

points: Classic: a menu bar and a toolbar.
Ribbon: large buttons in named groups, one tab for each menu. It can be collapsed to leave more room for the document.
Side panel: the tools in a panel on the left or on the right, which can be collapsed to icons.

body: Choose the layout of every app in Settings → General → Layout. An app can have a layout of its own, chosen in its part of Settings or from its View menu; it then no longer follows the general one until you choose "Use the general layout".

topics.title: Theme
body: Settings → General → Theme: Light, Dark, Light gray, Dark gray, or Automatic, which follows the light or dark setting of the system.
The pages of a document are never recoloured by the theme: paper stays as it is.

topics.title: Language
body: Settings → General → Language. The program speaks 62 languages. "System language" follows the language of your system. The list can be searched by a language's own name, its name in your language or its English name.
A text that is not translated yet is shown in English, never as a code.

topics.title: Tabs

points: The mark on a tab can be the icon of its app or a plain square in the app's colour.

body: When there are more tabs than fit, the arrows at the ends of the strip scroll it, and "More tabs" lists them all.

topics.title: Searching for a command
body: The search box ("Search commands and settings") finds any command of the tab in front by its name, in your language or in English. Choose a result to run it.
Commands that are planned but not written yet are shown greyed out in the menus and are left out of the search.

topics.title: Keyboard shortcuts
body: A command's keys are written beside its name in the menus and in its tooltip. The ones used most:

points: Ctrl+O: open a file
Ctrl+S: save; Ctrl+Shift+S: save as
Ctrl+P: print
Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y: undo and redo
Ctrl+F: find in the document
Ctrl+W: close the tab
Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab: the next tab and the one before
Ctrl+, (comma): Settings
F1: this Help
Escape: leave full screen or read mode, or put down the tool in hand

body: The keys of the program’s own commands (tabs, Settings, Help) are changed in Settings → General → Keyboard shortcuts; those of an app’s commands in its part of Settings. Click the keys of a command, then press the new ones.

topics.title: Using this Help
body: Help belongs to where you open it from. From an app you see only the manual of that app and the commands of the tab you came from. From Settings you see "About" (the program and each app, in short) and the manual of the program. Help → About always leads to "About".
The contents are on the left; the search above them looks through every topic, in titles and in text.

Help opens in a tab of its own, so you can go back and forth between it and your work; F1 brings it to the front again. Under "Commands of the tab you came from" every menu of that tab is listed with each of its commands, its keys and what it does: open Help from the tab you have a question about.

topics.title: The right-click menu of Windows Explorer
body: Settings → General → Windows Explorer → "Show Syntelab Creative in the right-click menu of files and folders" adds entries for the files the program reads: "Convert to PDF with PDF Organizer" and "Combine files in PDF Organizer", each with the icon of PDF Organizer, and "Syntelab Dev", which opens to the side with Checksums, Compare and Hex view.

They are added for your user alone, without administrator rights, and turning the switch off removes them. On Windows 11 they are under "Show more options". They always start the installed program: if it was moved or reinstalled elsewhere, it puts them right when it starts.

body.note: Choosing "Combine files in PDF Organizer" on several files opens a binder with them; "Convert to PDF with PDF Organizer" opens each file in a tab of its own as an unsaved PDF, written to disk only when you save it.

topics.title: What goes online, and what never does
body: The program collects nothing: no usage data, no file names, no crash reports sent by themselves.
It goes online only in these cases, each one asked for by you:

points: Checking for updates and news (two small files read from syntelab.com), when you ask or, if you allowed it, when the program starts; and downloading a new version, only when you press "Update".
Saving a web page as a PDF (PDF Organizer) and bringing the text of a web page (Scribe), from the address you typed.
A link in a document that you click: it is handed to your browser or mail program.
Feedback and Support: they open a page of syntelab.com in your browser.

body: Signing with a certificate and checking signatures are done on your computer, without going online.

topics.title: Updates
body: Settings → General → Updates → "Check for updates". When a newer version exists, a window tells you what is new and offers "Update".

"Update" downloads the new version, checks that it really comes from us (it must be signed with our key; anything else is refused) and installs it over this one. Your settings are kept and the program starts again. Nothing is downloaded until you press it.

If the update cannot be installed this way (a portable copy, a Linux package, no network), "Download" opens the download page in your browser; install the new version over this one and your settings are kept.
"Check for updates and news when the program starts" can be turned off; nothing about you or your computer is sent either way.

topics.title: Feedback and support
body: Help → Feedback: ask for a new app, a new feature or a change, or report a problem. Every message is read.
Help → Support: the program is free; this is where you can help it go on.

topics.title: About Syntelab Creative
body: Syntelab Creative is a free suite of apps for everyday work with documents, text and data, made by Syntelab (syntelab.com). It starts with four apps: PDF Organizer, Scribe, Units and Dev. Others will join them in the same window.

points: Always free.
No data collected: nothing about you, your computer or your work.
Nothing held back: no paid version, no feature locked, no limit put there on purpose. The only limits are what today’s technology can do and what your computer can carry.

body: We have no funding. The program is made in our free time, as far as that time allows. We fully intend to make software of good quality, and that takes time and patience: ours to build it, and yours while it grows.
It will get better with every version. Problems that are reported get corrected, and features that are asked for are weighed for what comes next.

body.note: Your documents stay on your computer. The program collects nothing about you or your work; see "What goes online, and what never does".

topics.title: How you can help
body: There are three ways, and each of them counts:

points: Tell us what you think: Help → Feedback. A problem you ran into, something that is missing, something that is harder than it should be. We read every message.

Tell others about the program and what we do. More people using it means more feedback, and that is how we see what really matters. It also makes us feel that our work is appreciated: ours, and that of everyone who takes part in the project and will take part in it.
Support it with money, if you can: Help → Support us. It buys us time to work on it.

body: None of this is asked of you. The program is free and will always be free, whole, for everyone.

topics.title: What it is built with
body: The program stands on the work of many people. What every app shares:

points: The window and everything you see: Tauri, with the web view of the system (WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux, WKWebView on macOS); written in TypeScript with React.
The part that does the work: written in Rust.
Letters and icons: Sansation, IBM Plex Sans and Font Awesome Free.

body: What each app adds is said on its own page under "About". We are grateful to the people behind these projects.

topics.title: What it cannot do yet
body: So that you know before you count on it:

points: Some texts are still waiting for their translation. Until then they are shown in English, never as a code.
The right-click menu of the file manager is there only in Windows Explorer for now.
Signing with a certificate works on Windows for now; on Linux and macOS it will come in a later version.

body: The limits of each app are on its own page under "About". If one of them stands in your way, tell us through Help → Feedback: it helps us decide what comes first.

topics.title: What we are working on
body: The four apps will keep growing: what you report and ask for through Help → Feedback decides much of what comes first. Beside them, new apps are being prepared. The list of apps does not show them unless you want to: tick them in its "View" menu to see them there as "Coming soon":

points: Convert: converting files from one format to another, among them office documents to PDF and back, without needing another program to be installed. We have not yet found an open technology that reaches the quality we want, so it will come only when it does not disappoint you; where the tools do not exist, we will build them.
Pixel: tools for images, such as resizing and compressing, removing a background, colours and QR codes.
Metadata: seeing and removing the hidden data of photos, videos and documents, before you share them.
Wizard: random pickers and generators: a wheel to spin, dice, a coin, names drawn from a list.

body: In the apps that are already here we are working on what their "What it cannot do yet" pages list: for example a trusted timestamp for signatures, signing with a certificate on Linux and macOS, and a spelling check in Scribe.
More install choices will follow as well: Microsoft Store and winget on Windows, Flathub and Snap on Linux.

body.note: News of each version is under the news button on the side bar; Settings → General → Updates checks for a newer version.

topics.title: The first page
body: A Dev tab opens on the first page, where every tool is, grouped as in the menus: Encode, Data, Generate, Inspect, Network.

points: Type in "Find a tool" to narrow the list.
The pin on a tool keeps it at the top, under Pinned.
A tool opens in the same tab; File → All tools goes back to the first page. In Settings you can have each tool open in a tab of its own, and a new tab open on the tool used last.

topics.title: Paste anything
body: The box at the top of the first page takes whatever you paste and says what it looks like: a token, a certificate, JSON, UUIDs, timestamps, cron schedules, URLs, XML or HTML, SQL, Base64, a checksum, a table, YAML.
Under each guess are the tools that work on such a thing, the best fit first. Click one: it opens with the text already in it and run.

body.note: What you paste stays in the box until you clear it or close the tab. It is never written to disk.

topics.title: How a tool is laid out
body: Most tools have the same frame: the options in a line at the top, the input on one side, the output on the other, and a line at the bottom that says what happened.

points: The result is made again whenever the input or an option changes, and shown in the output; "Runs by itself" in the line of options says so. Only a text too long to run at every key, or a file larger than 128 MB, waits for the Run button, which shows then. Ctrl+Enter runs the tool at any time.

A result that is not text (a picture decoded from Base64, gzip) is shown as a preview: a picture as it is, anything else by its kind, its size and its first bytes. Copy then copies it as Base64, and a picture can be copied as a picture. So is an input file that is not text.
Open a file, Paste and Clear are over the input; Copy and Save to a file over the output. A file can also be dropped on the input.
What is wrong with the input is said in words, with its line and column, and marked in the editor.
The View menu puts the two panes side by side or one under the other, shows line numbers and wraps long lines; the line between the panes can be dragged.
The options you choose are remembered for the next time. What you type is not.

topics.title: Burn, and what is kept
body: Burn, at the bottom right of every tool, empties it at once: the input, the result, anything typed in its boxes, and what its editors could undo.

Dev keeps only its settings, the tools you pinned, the name of the tool used last and the options of each tool. Nothing you type, paste, open or make in a tool is written to disk, to a log or to a list of recent things. Secrets least of all: keys, passphrases, tokens and the headers of a request live in the tab and nowhere else.

One thing waits on disk for a while: the result of a file, and a result that is not text, are written to a folder of the program’s own so they can be shown and then saved. Each is deleted when another result takes its place, when you burn the tool or close it, and in any case when Dev starts again.

topics.title: Files of any size
body: There is no limit put on the size of a file. A file small enough to be shown (up to 16 MB) is put in the editor. A larger one, or one that is not text, stays on disk: its start (or a preview) is shown, the tool reads it from where it is, and its result is shown as for a text. Save to a file then copies the result where you choose.

points: Long work shows a card with how far it has got and a Stop button.
A file that is text in another encoding than UTF-8 (UTF-16, Windows-1252 and the like) is read as text when it is small enough to be shown, and the encoding is said. What you save from Dev is UTF-8.
A file dropped on a tool is opened as with Open a file. Where the window cannot tell where it is, it is taken up to 16 MB, as if pasted.

topics.title: Many files and whole folders
body: Where a tool has "Work on: Text / Files", Files runs it on many files in one go.

steps: Add files, or a folder (with the folders under it, if you leave that on).
Each file is read once as it is added and told whether the tool takes it.

Choose where the results go: beside each file under a new name, into a folder (keeping the folders), or over the files themselves, which asks you once more. Hash can also just show the results in the list.
Click a file in the list to see its result alone under the choices, before anything is written.
Run. A file that is wrong does not stop the others; each says how it came out.

body.note: A result never lands on a file that is already there unless you ask for that.

topics.title: The right-click menu of Windows Explorer
body: Turn it on in the Settings of the program, under Windows Explorer. Everything is gathered under one line, "Syntelab Creative"; on Windows 11 it is under "Show more options".

points: Open in Syntelab Dev: on the kinds of files a tool reads (.json, .yaml, .xml, .html, .sql, .csv, .pem, .crt, .der, .pfx, .key, .csr, .gz and the like). The file opens in the tool for its kind.
Checksums: on any file or folder. The digests are listed, each beside its file, and nothing is written.
Hex view: on any file.
Compare: two files go into the two sides of Diff; two folders into the comparison of folders.

topics.title: Base64
body: Turns bytes into Base64 and back. Encoding takes any file; decoding gives back the bytes, shown when they are text and saved to a file when they are not.

points: Alphabet: the standard one, or the one for URLs (- and _).
Fill with =, and lines of 64, 76 or any number of letters.
Decoding takes both alphabets, with or without the filling, and says where a letter is wrong.

topics.title: URL encode / decode
body: Percent-encoding, as browsers write it: a part of an address (everything that is not a plain letter is encoded), a whole address (its own signs are kept), or a form (+ for a space).
Decoding says where a % is not followed by two hexadecimal digits.

topics.title: HTML entities
body: Writes the signs HTML and XML keep for themselves (&, <, >, quotes) as entities, and reads entities back: by name, by decimal number or by hexadecimal number. The names are those of the HTML standard.
"Every letter that is not ASCII too" writes accented letters and other alphabets as entities as well.

topics.title: JWT decoder
body: Takes a JSON Web Token apart: its header and its payload as JSON, and its claims in words (issuer, subject, audience, when it expires, with "expired" or "not expired yet").
Give the secret to check a signature made with a shared secret (HS256, HS384, HS512). Signatures made with a private key (RS, ES, PS) are not checked.

body.note: The token and the secret stay in the tab: nothing is sent anywhere to decode a token.

topics.title: Escape / unescape
body: Writes a text as a string of a language (JSON, JavaScript, C, C++, Java and the like) with its quotes, line breaks and other signs escaped, and reads such a string back.

topics.title: Gzip
body: Compresses and decompresses gzip, a file of any size as it is read. The level goes from fastest to smallest; the result of a text can be given as Base64.

topics.title: Number bases
body: Tells whole numbers, one on each line, in binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal, and in one more base of your choosing, up to 36. A number has no largest size.

points: The base of a number is told from how it is written: 0x for hexadecimal, 0b for binary, 0o for octal, letters for hexadecimal, decimal otherwise. Or choose the base everything is read in.
Spaces, underscores and apostrophes between digits are passed over: 1_000_000.
A negative number is also given as computers keep it (two’s complement), in the smallest of 8, 16, 32, 64 bits and so on that holds it.

topics.title: JSON formatter
body: Formats, minifies and validates JSON, and shows it as a tree. A document of any size is read as a stream.

points: Indent with 2 or 4 spaces, a tab, or any number of spaces.
More options: sort keys, short lists on one line, the space after the colon, how lines end, a line break at the end, non-ASCII letters as \uXXXX.
Lenient reading takes comments (// and /* */) and trailing commas, and writes strict JSON.
Changes: drop nulls, drop empty values and the like, in one pass.
The tree opens a level at a time and finds a text in keys and values.

topics.title: JSONPath
body: Runs a JSONPath query (RFC 9535) on a document: $.store.book[?@.price < 10].title. The result is the values found, the paths to them, or both.
A query that is wrong is said with the place it goes wrong at.

topics.title: JSON Schema validator
body: Checks a document against a JSON Schema (drafts 4 to 2020-12). The schema goes in the pane under the input. Each thing that does not fit is listed with where it is and the rule it breaks.
On many files, each is checked against the same schema. A $ref to another file or to an address is not followed.

topics.title: Schema generator and JSON to TypeScript
body: From a sample of JSON, the schema generator writes a JSON Schema it fits, and JSON to TypeScript writes the declarations of its type (interfaces or types, exported or not, readonly or not, under a name you give).

topics.title: YAML ↔ JSON
body: Turns YAML into JSON and JSON into YAML. YAML is read by its core schema, with anchors and merges followed; what is wrong is said with its place.

topics.title: CSV ↔ JSON
body: Turns a table into JSON and back. The separator is told from the first row, or chosen (comma, semicolon, tab, pipe); the first row may be the header; numbers and true / false may be detected.
"Table" shows the CSV in rows and columns, a file of any size.

topics.title: XML / HTML formatter
body: Formats, minifies and checks XML and HTML. XML is read strictly: a tag that is never closed is said with its place. HTML is read as browsers forgive it.

topics.title: SQL formatter
body: Lays a statement out, a clause to a line, or puts it on one line; keywords in capitals, in small letters or as written. It asks for no dialect and does not check what a statement means.

topics.title: Diff
body: Compares two texts line by line, two JSON documents by what they say, or two folders file by file. The first goes in the input, the second in the pane under it.

points: Side by side marks the words that changed inside a line; Unified is a patch as diff -u writes it.
Ignore case, whitespace, empty lines, digits or punctuation.
For JSON, the order of keys and the layout are no difference; the result can be a JSON Patch (RFC 6902).
Folders: which files only one has, which are the same, which differ; Compare on a row opens the pair as texts.

topics.title: Markdown preview
body: Shows Markdown as it will look, and gives its HTML to copy or save: CommonMark with tables, strikethrough, task lists and footnotes.

points: HTML typed inside the Markdown is shown as text, not run.
A picture that would be fetched from the network is not fetched: its description and address are shown in its place. A picture carried in the text (data:) is shown.
A link you click opens in the browser of the system.

topics.title: UUID
body: Makes UUIDs of versions 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 (RFC 9562), as many as you ask for, written with hyphens, plain, as a URN or in braces. "Take apart" tells the version of each UUID and the time or the name inside it.

topics.title: Hash
body: CRC-32, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 of a text or a file, several at once, written as hex or Base64. A file of any size is hashed as it is read.

points: Check against: paste a checksum, or the line of a .sha256 file; it is told to match or not.
HMAC key: the digests become HMACs with that key.
Each line apart: one digest for each line of the text.
Files: the digests are listed beside their files; Copy all gives them as sha256sum writes them.

topics.title: Passwords and secrets
body: Makes passwords of the kinds of letters you choose, passphrases of words, and random bytes as hex or Base64, from the random numbers of the operating system. Each says how many bits of entropy it has. Once something is made, changing an option makes it again.
A passphrase is words drawn from the long word list of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (7776 English words), each as likely as the others: six words are about 77 bits.

topics.title: Keys and certificates
body: Five things, chosen at the top:

points: New key: RSA, EC P-256 / P-384 / P-521 or Ed25519, given in every form programs take (PKCS #8, the older form, OpenSSH; the public key as PEM and as the line for authorized_keys), locked with a passphrase if you give one.
Certificate request: a CSR for a new key or one you paste, with its subject and its other names (SAN).
Self-signed certificate: the same, signed with its own key, for so many days; "It may sign other certificates" makes it an authority of your own.
Sign with your own CA: paste a request, the certificate of your authority and its key; you get the signed certificate and the authority after it.

Read and convert: paste or open anything (PEM, DER, an OpenSSH key, a .pfx or .p12 file, locked or not). It says what it found and whether the key is the one of the certificate, and writes each thing in the other forms. A key and its certificate can be saved together as a .pfx.

body.note: Everything is made on this computer. A key is in the tab until Burn, and nowhere else unless you save it.

topics.title: Regex tester
body: Tries a regular expression of JavaScript on a text: the matches with their groups and places, or the text with the matches replaced. The flags are g, i, m, s, u, y.
The pattern runs apart from the window, and one that runs longer than 20 seconds is ended.

topics.title: Cron explain
body: Says in words what a schedule means and when it runs: crontab (five fields, six with seconds, seven with a year), Quartz, AWS EventBridge cron() and rate(), and systemd OnCalendar. One schedule to a line.

points: The next runs, and the previous ones when asked, in the time zone you choose.

Days of the week are numbered from 0 for Sunday, or from 1 as Quartz numbers them, as you choose. A line with seconds that also has a year, L, W or # is of Quartz, and is read the Quartz way by itself.
The same schedule in the other forms, to copy or to add to the input.
The builder makes a schedule by choosing each field; "Change in the builder" takes a typed schedule up in it.

topics.title: Unix timestamp
body: Reads moments, one to a line: seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds since 1970, or a date written in the usual ways (ISO 8601, as mail and HTTP write it, as Git writes it). Each is told in the time zone you choose, in UTC, and as every kind of timestamp.

topics.title: URL parser
body: Takes a URL apart as browsers read it: scheme, user, host (with its Unicode form when it is written in punycode), port, path, each parameter of the query decoded, and the fragment.

topics.title: Certificate decoder
body: Reads X.509 certificates from PEM or DER and tells everything in them: subject, issuer, validity, the names it is for, its key, its extensions and its fingerprints.
It reads; it does not judge whether a certificate is to be trusted. For the certificate a site shows, and whether this computer trusts it, use Network → Certificate of a site.

topics.title: Hex viewer
body: Shows the bytes of a file of any size, or of a pasted text: the position of each row, the bytes, and the same bytes as letters.

points: Go to a position written as 0x1F4, 1F4h or 500.
Find bytes (DE AD BE EF) or a text (UTF-8, or UTF-16 either way round), forward and back.
Click a byte: the side shows what is there as numbers of every size, in either byte order, as a character and as a time.
Select with a drag, Shift or the arrow keys; copy the selection as hex, as code, as Base64 or as text, or save it to a file.

body.note: It only looks: nothing is changed in the file.

topics.title: Where the network tools go
body: These four tools are the only part of Dev that goes online, and they go where you point them.

points: Only the address you type is contacted, and only when you press the button. Never in the background.
What is sent is what you wrote. The only thing added to a request is a User-Agent that is the same for everyone ("Syntelab Creative"), unless you give your own.
No cookies are kept, nothing about you or the computer is sent, and nothing typed is kept.

topics.title: HTTP client
body: Sends one request written by hand: method, address, headers (one to a line: Name: value) and a body, typed or taken from a file of any size.

points: The answer: its number, how long it took (in all, and to the first byte), its size, its headers, and its body, coloured by its kind and laid out when it is JSON. A body that is not text (a picture, a PDF) is shown as it is, and saved as it came.
Follow redirects, or see the first answer as it is. The addresses a request was sent on from are listed.
Check the certificate against what this computer trusts; turn it off only for servers of your own.
"Send, answer to a file" writes a body of any size straight to disk, with progress and Stop.
"Copy as curl" gives the same request as a command.

topics.title: DNS lookup
body: Asks a name server for the records of a name: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, SOA, PTR, SRV, CAA, DS, DNSKEY, several at once. An address gives its name (PTR).
The question goes to the name server the computer is set to use, to a public one (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9), to a resolver over HTTPS (Cloudflare, Google), or to one you type.

topics.title: Port check
body: Tells whether ports of a host take TCP connections: one, several, or a range up to all 65 535 (22, 80, 443, 8000-8100). Each is open, closed, or without an answer in the time you give.

body.note: Try only hosts that are yours, or that you may test.

topics.title: Certificate of a site
body: Shows the certificates a site gives when a secure connection is made: whom they are for, who signed them, how many days are left, whether this computer trusts them and why not, the version of TLS and the cipher. Only the handshake is done: no request is sent.

points: Write example.com, example.com:8443 or a web address.
Mail servers and FTP begin in the clear and are asked to go over to TLS (STARTTLS): chosen by the port (25, 587, 143, 110, 21) or by hand.
"Everything" shows all that the certificates say; "PEM" gives them to copy or save.

topics.title: The settings of Dev
body: File → Settings opens the Settings of the program at the part of Dev.

points: Open each tool in a tab of its own, or in the tab it is chosen in.
Open a new tab on the tool used last, or on the first page.
Put back the options of every tool, and the pins, as the program ships.

body: The right-click menu of Windows Explorer, the language, the theme and the keys are in the Settings of the program as a whole.

topics.title: About Dev
body: Dev is the app of Syntelab Creative for developers: tools that encode and decode, format and check, turn one form of data into another, and take apart what is hard to read as it is.

Everything is done on this computer. Nothing you type, paste or open in a tool is kept or sent anywhere. There is no limit put on the size or the number of files: the limits are the memory and the disk of the computer.
It is new and still being built. Where it falls short for your work, tell us through Help → Feedback.

Apache-2.0 or MIT licence. Copyright (c) 2020-2023 The RustCrypto Project Developers.
