The words of passphrases: the EFF Large Wordlist for Passphrases, https://www.eff.org/dice , by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, used under the Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 United States licence ( https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/us/ ). The list is used as it is.
Opening keys locked the old way of OpenSSL: aes, cbc and des of RustCrypto, https://github.com/RustCrypto . MIT or Apache-2.0 licence. Copyright (c) RustCrypto Developers.
Written for Dev, with no library: the DNS lookup (questions written and answers read as RFC 1035 has them) and the port check.

Written for Dev, with no library: reading and writing JSON as a stream, JSONPath (RFC 9535), Base64, percent-encoding, HTML character references (their names are those of the HTML standard, https://html.spec.whatwg.org ), string escapes, reading JSON Web Tokens, writing YAML, CSV both ways, reading cron schedules, the XML and HTML formatter, and the SQL formatter.

body: What it shares with the rest of the program is under "About Syntelab Creative".

points: The signature of a token is checked only when it was made with a shared secret (HS256, HS384, HS512).
The JSON Schema validator says what does not fit in English, as its library does, and does not follow a $ref to another file or address.
The SQL formatter asks for no dialect and does not check what a statement means: it tells only of a string or a comment that never ends.
YAML, and JSON that becomes YAML or CSV, are held whole in memory while they are turned; CSV that becomes JSON, XML, HTML and SQL are worked on as they are read, whatever their size.
The table CSV is looked at in is read only: nothing is typed in it, and nothing is copied from it yet.
Diff keeps sixteen bytes for each line of the two files, not the files themselves; two JSON documents are held whole, since they are written anew before they are compared.
A stretch of lines with nothing both sides have exactly once is compared as well as a second allows: the differences told are true, though not always the fewest.
Diff does not compare how lines end (CRLF or LF).
Two folders are compared by the bytes of their files; files are matched by their names, letter for letter.
What the Inspect tools tell is JSON, with its names in English.

The regex tester runs the regular expressions of JavaScript, not PCRE and not those of Rust; it works on a text that can be shown, not on a file kept on disk; a pattern that runs longer than 20 seconds is ended.
The certificate decoder reads a certificate and does not check whether it is to be trusted: not its chain, not its signature, not whether it was revoked.
A file that is text in another encoding than UTF-8 is read when it is small enough to be shown; one larger than that, worked on from disk, must be UTF-8.
A file dropped on a tool is taken up to 16 MB; the window is not told where a dropped file is on disk, so a larger one is opened with Open a file.
Passphrases are made of English words only.

Cron explain: the builder makes crontab schedules (five fields, or six with seconds); a schedule with L, W, # or ? cannot be taken up in it. The times of an AWS rate() cannot be told, since it is counted from when its rule was made. Of systemd, the common calendar events are read; not fractions of a second or lists of days counted from the end of the month.
Hex viewer only looks: nothing is changed in the file. The column of text shows ASCII or the Western European letters, not other alphabets; bytes or a text are sought, not patterns.

Keys and certificates: keys are RSA, the curves P-256, P-384 and P-521, and Ed25519; others (DSA, secp256k1, X25519) are not read. A key locked the old way of OpenSSL is opened when its cipher is AES or 3DES. A .pfx file holds one key with its certificates. Making a very large RSA key takes time and cannot be stopped halfway. The library that makes RSA keys has a known weakness to an attacker who can time many signatures over a network (RUSTSEC-2023-0071): here keys are made and written on your computer, and nothing is signed for anyone else.

HTTP client: HTTP/1.1 (not HTTP/2 or 3); no cookies are kept between requests; forms of several parts (multipart) are not built for you; an answer larger than 16 MB, or one that is not text, is written to a file by sending the request again.

DNS lookup shows signatures (DNSSEC) and does not check them. Port check tries TCP only: a UDP port that is silent cannot be told from one that is closed. Certificate of a site does not ask whether a certificate was revoked.
The right-click menu is for Windows Explorer; on Windows 11 its entries are under "Show more options".

topics.title: Opening a document
body: File → Open (Ctrl+O) opens a PDF in a tab of its own. "Open several files at once" opens each chosen file in its tab.

Files that are not PDFs open too, as pages: pictures (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, WebP and many more), text and web files, e-books, XPS, and office documents. Such a document is not saved anywhere yet: "Save" asks where.

body.note: Office documents (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument) are converted by Word, Excel or PowerPoint, or by LibreOffice, whichever is on the computer. Without one of them they cannot be opened.

body: Files dropped on the window open each in its own tab, as with Open; a file that is not a PDF opens as an unsaved PDF made from it. Dropped among the small pages beside a document, or among the pages in Organize, their pages are added there.

On Windows, PDF Organizer can be the app that opens PDF files when you double-click them: on its start page, "Make default" opens the Windows settings, where you choose Syntelab Creative for PDF files.

topics.title: Looking at the pages
body: The View menu decides how the document is shown; nothing in it changes the file.

points: Zoom: in, out, actual size, fit the page, fit the width, fit the height. Ctrl and the mouse wheel zoom too.
Page display: one page or two side by side, with or without a cover page, and scrolling through all pages as one long strip.
Guides: rulers and a grid, in the unit chosen in Settings.
"Show thumbnails": the small pages on the side. Click one to go to it; the bookmarks of the document are in the same panel.
"Read mode" hides the tools; "Full screen mode" hides everything but the page. Escape leaves both.

body: The strip above the pages (the quick toolbar) has the page number, the zoom and the buttons you chose in Settings.

topics.title: Finding text
body: Edit → Find in document (Ctrl+F): type a word or a phrase; the places it is found are marked on the pages, and the arrows go from one to the next.

body.note: A scanned document is pictures of pages and has no text to find until its text is recognized: see "Recognizing text (OCR)".

topics.title: Document properties
body: File → Document properties shows what the document says about itself: title, author, the dates it was made and changed, the number of pages, the size of the file.

topics.title: Save and Save as
body: Nothing you do changes the file on disk until you save. Until then, every step can be undone (Ctrl+Z) and redone (Ctrl+Y).

points: Save (Ctrl+S) writes the document over its file.
Save as (Ctrl+Shift+S) writes it to a new file, which then takes the tab's place; the old file stays as it was.

body: If another program has the file open, it cannot be written over: the program says so and keeps your changes, to be saved under another name.

body.note: Saving a changed document over a file that is signed with a certificate removes its signatures. The program asks first and offers "Save as a new file"; the question can be turned off in Settings → Signatures.

topics.title: Creating a PDF
body: File → Create a PDF makes a new document:

points: from one file, or from several: combined into one PDF, or one PDF for each;
from a web page, at the address you type (the page is saved with the browser installed on the computer);
from what is on the clipboard;
from empty pages of the size you choose.

topics.title: Exporting to another format
body: File → Export writes the document in another format: Word or OpenDocument text, plain text, a web page, XML, pictures of the pages (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, SVG) or PostScript. For pictures you choose the resolution.
The document itself stays a PDF; the export is a new file.

body.note: Text can only be exported where the document has text. Recognize the text of a scan first.

topics.title: Printing
body: File → Print (Ctrl+P) prints the document as it is arranged now, with what you drew on it. Choose the pages, the paper, whether sheets lie upright or sideways, and whether pages are fitted to the sheet or printed at their real size; then the system's print window asks for the printer.
The paper, orientation and scaling the print window starts with are set in Settings → Printing.

topics.title: Sharing
body: File → Share hands the document to the "Share" window of the system: mail, a nearby device and other apps. The document is shared as it is now, with your unsaved changes.

topics.title: The Organize view
body: Organize → Organize pages shows every page in a grid. Nothing changes on disk until you save.

points: Select: click a page; Ctrl+click adds one, Shift+click takes a run. "Select all pages", "Select none", "Select odd pages" and "Select even pages" are in the menu.
Move: drag the selected pages to their new place, or use "Move left" and "Move right".
Turn: "Selected: rotate left" and "Selected: rotate right" turn the selected pages; "All pages: rotate left" and "All pages: rotate right" turn every page.
Delete: the Delete key, or "Delete pages". A document keeps at least one page.
Copy, cut and paste (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V): pages can be pasted in the same document or in another one open in the program.
Size: the slider at the top makes the pages larger or smaller; so do Ctrl + mouse wheel over the pages, and Zoom in and Zoom out (Ctrl+= and Ctrl+-). The size is remembered.

body: The same commands work without the grid, on the page in view.

topics.title: Extracting pages and splitting a document
body: Organize → Extract pages takes the selected pages out as a new document in its own tab, not saved yet. You can also have each page written as a file of its own, and choose whether the pages are removed from this document.
Organize → Split document writes the document as several smaller files; this document stays as it is.
The names of the new documents follow the patterns in Settings → Names of new documents.

body.note: Signatures made with a certificate are not carried into extracted or split documents: a signature is good only for the file it was made in.

points: Organize → Insert pages adds the pages of another file (PDF, picture, text, office document) after the selected page, or at the end.
Organize → Replace pages puts the pages of another file in place of the selected ones.
Insert → Blank page adds an empty page of the size of its neighbour.

topics.title: Cropping and resizing pages
body: Edit → Crop pages cuts the edges off pages, by margins you type or drag. Nothing is removed from the file: the pages only show less.
Edit → Resize pages puts pages on another sheet size (A4, Letter and others). The content can be scaled to fit or kept at its size, and placed at one of nine places on the new sheet.
Both ask which pages: all, the selected ones, a range, odd or even.

topics.title: The binder
body: Combine → New binder opens a place to gather files and write them as one PDF.

steps: Add files with "Add files", or drop them on the binder. PDFs, pictures, text and office documents can be mixed.
Drag the cards into the order you want, or use the arrows on each card.
Open a card to choose which of its pages go in.
"Combine files" writes them, in order, as one new document in its own tab.

body: The files themselves are not changed.
The slider at the top makes the pages on the cards larger or smaller; so do Ctrl + mouse wheel, and Zoom in and Zoom out (Ctrl+= and Ctrl+-). The size is remembered.

topics.title: The tools
body: The drawing tools open as a panel beside the page, as a grid of buttons or as a list with names (Settings decides). With a tool in hand, drag or click on the page; Escape puts the tool down.

points: Text: click and type. Font, size, colour, bold, italic and alignment are in the panel.
Image: choose a picture, then drag where it goes and how large.
Shapes: rectangle, ellipse, line, arrow, tick, cross, dot.
Highlight: drag over what should stand out; what is under it stays readable.

body: With "Select, move and resize" a mark is picked up again: drag it, pull its corners, turn it by its handle, change its colours in the panel, or delete it with the Delete key. Marks can be copied and pasted, also to other pages.
Everything drawn is written into the file when you save.

topics.title: Changing the document's own text and pictures
body: The tool "Edit the text and pictures of the document" outlines what the page itself has. Click a line of text to rewrite it, or a picture to move, resize, turn or delete it.

body.note: This changes one line or one picture at a time. Paragraphs do not flow again when a line gets longer, and a picture that lies over another is picked up together with it. For large changes, edit the document in the program it was written in.

topics.title: Redacting
body: More tools → Redact removes for good what must not be read: drag a black box over it, on any page. When you save, the text and pictures under the box are taken out of the file, not merely covered.

body.note: Save the redacted document under a new name and keep the original somewhere safe: what is redacted cannot be brought back.

topics.title: Watermark
body: Edit → Watermark writes words or puts a picture on the pages you choose: straight or slanted, at one of nine places, as large and as faint as you set. On each page it is then a mark like any other and can still be moved or removed.

topics.title: Page numbers, header and footer, Bates numbers

points: Edit → Page numbers: the format (1, 1 / 12, Page 1 and others), the place, and which pages get one.

Insert → Header and footer: text at any of six places. In it, {page} stands for the number of the page, {pages} for the number of pages, {date} for today's date and {file} for the name of the document.
Insert → Bates numbering: numbers one after another with a word before or after (ABC000123), as used for the documents of a case.

topics.title: Links
body: Insert → Link: drag over the place that should be clicked, then say where it leads: a web address, or a page of this document.
Links of a document work while you read it: a click on a link to a page goes there; a web or mail address is handed to your browser or mail program.

topics.title: Bookmarks
body: Insert → New bookmark: click the place it should lead to and give it a title. Insert → Bookmarks opens the list, where a bookmark can be renamed or removed. The changes are written when you save.

topics.title: Attached files
body: Insert → Attach a file: choose a file and click where its paper clip goes. You can give it a name and an author, colour the clip, resize and turn it. The file is kept inside the PDF when you save.
Insert → Attached files lists what the document carries; each file can be saved to disk or taken out. A click on a paper clip opens the same list.

topics.title: Filling in a form
body: Insert → Fill in form shows the fields of the document: type in text fields, tick boxes, choose from lists. The answers are written into the file when you save.

topics.title: Making a form
body: The Insert menu adds fields to any document: a text field, a check box, radio buttons (of which one can be chosen), a list to choose from, and a signature field left empty for a signer.
Drag on the page where the field goes. Like other marks, a field can be moved and resized until you save; after that it is part of the form.

topics.title: Adding a signature you draw
body: Sign → Add signature puts the picture of a signature on the page: drawn here with a pen you choose, typed in a font, or taken from a picture (with "Keep the pen strokes only" for a photo of a signed sheet). The date can be written under it.
Drag on the page where it goes. Signatures you used are kept on this computer, to be used again.

body.note: This is a picture: it says nothing certain about who put it there. A signature that proves who signed, and that nothing changed since, is made with a certificate.

topics.title: Signing with a certificate
body: Sign → Sign with certificate makes a digital signature: it says who signed and seals the document, so any later change shows.

steps: Drag on the page the area where the signature shows (a window says so first; it can be turned off). To sign without anything on the pages, choose "Sign without showing it on a page" instead.
Choose the certificate: one of the computer's (a card or a token shows among them once it is in its reader), or a .pfx / .p12 file with its password. "Continue".

Choose the appearance of the signature. Under "Reason and place" you can write why and where you sign: they go into the signature, and onto the page if the appearance shows them. Tick "Lock the document after signing" if no one should sign or change it after you. Leave "Add a trusted time (time stamp)" ticked so that an authority confirms when you signed.
"Sign", then choose where the signed file is saved. A token asks for its PIN at this point.

body: The signed file opens in place of the document. A password or a PIN is never kept by the program.

body.note: A qualified signature is one made this way with a qualified certificate, on its card or token. Signing is done on your computer; only the time stamp and the check of your certificate go online, and they send fingerprints and the certificate’s serial number, never the document.

topics.title: Signature appearances
body: An appearance says how a certificate signature looks on the page. Keep several under names of your own: one for signing for a company, one for signing in your own name.

points: Picture: none, from a file (a stamp, a scanned signature) or drawn here.
Text shown: name, date, reason, place, each with or without its label.
Lines of your own under the name, such as a role and a company.
"Standard text" is always there: who signed and when.

body: In the signing window: "New…", "Edit…", "Delete". The last one used is offered first. Appearances are kept on this computer.

topics.title: Several signatures, and locking
body: A document can be signed by several people, one after another. Open the signed file and sign it without changing anything: your signature is added to the end of the file and the earlier ones stay good.
"Lock the document after signing" (off unless you tick it) closes the document: no one can sign after you and nothing more may be changed. It cannot be undone.

body.note: If you change a signed document before signing it again, it has to be written anew and the earlier signatures are left out. The signing window warns you: to keep them, open the file again and sign without changing anything.

topics.title: Time stamps
body: A time stamp is a time-stamping authority's signed word on when something was. The time in a signature otherwise comes from the clock of the signer's computer, which anyone can set; a time stamp proves the moment, and keeps the signature provable after the certificate expires (PAdES B-T).

points: Signatures get one when "Add a trusted time (time stamp)" is ticked in the signing window. Settings → Signatures says whether it starts ticked, here and in batch processing.

Sign → Add timestamp gives the whole document a time stamp of its own, without a certificate: it proves the document was, exactly as it is, at that moment. It is saved as a new file; signatures the file has stay good.

body: The authority is DigiCert's (http://timestamp.digicert.com), free and trusted by Adobe Reader and Windows; another can be set in Settings → Signatures. It receives only a fingerprint (SHA-256), never the document, and an internet connection is needed. When a signature gets a time stamp, the issuer of your certificate is also asked whether the certificate is still valid, and its answer is kept in the signature (long-term validation): Adobe Reader can then show the signature as valid, now and after the certificate expires.

body.note: If the authority cannot be reached, nothing is signed or written: try again, or untick the time stamp to sign without it.

topics.title: Checking signatures
body: Sign → Verify signatures lists every certificate signature of the file: who signed, who issued the certificate, when, the reason and place, and

points: whether the document is unchanged since that signature (another signature added afterwards does not count as a change);
whether the signature locks the document;
whether this computer trusts the authority behind the certificate, and whether the certificate is valid today;
the time confirmed by its time stamp, and by which authority, when it has one. A time stamp of the whole document is listed too, with its own check.

body: The check is of the file as it was last saved and is done on this computer, without going online. Clicking a signature on a page opens this list at it. Under each signature, Show certificate opens the Windows window of the certificate (its chain and every detail; from there, Install Certificate makes this computer trust a certificate you know), and Validate asks the issuer of the certificate online, only when you press it, whether the certificate has been revoked.

topics.title: Recognizing text (OCR)
body: More tools → Recognize text (OCR) reads the words of scanned pages and writes them into the pages unseen, so the document can be searched and its text copied and exported. What the pages look like does not change.
Tick only the languages the pages are written in; pages that already have text are left as they are.

body.note: Reading is done by the Tesseract engine, a free program installed apart. Without it, the window shows the command that installs it on Windows.

topics.title: Making a document smaller
body: More tools → Compress saves the document as a smaller file by giving its photographs and scans fewer pixels. Three strengths; text and drawings stay as sharp as they are. A document with few pictures gains little.

topics.title: Comparing two documents
body: More tools → Compare documents: choose another PDF. The two are shown side by side, page by page, with the pages whose text differs marked and the lines each has alone listed.

topics.title: Batch processing: many files at once
body: More tools → Batch processing does the same things to many files, in a tab of its own. Each result is a new file. If results would take the place of files already in the folder (your own files, when they go to their folder with nothing added to their names), you are first asked whether to replace them, skip them, or cancel. A file is replaced only once its result is complete; one that is open (in a tab here or in another program) is left as it is and marked as not done.

steps: On the left, add the files: "Add files", "Add a folder" (with the folders under it), or drop them in.

On the right, tick what to do. Every file becomes a PDF in any case; besides that you can turn pages, recognize text, add a header and footer, a watermark or page numbers, make files smaller, sign them with a certificate, or write them out in another format. The numbers show the order.

Choose what is written: a file for each one, or everything in one PDF (in the order of the list), and the folder the results go to. When all the files come from one folder, that folder is chosen for you until you choose another; otherwise it is the last folder you chose.
"Start". Each file shows how it went; the run can be stopped between files.

points: Recipes: "Save as a recipe" keeps everything you chose (except the files and any password) under a name, to be set again with one choice.
"Keep the folders of the files in the results" rebuilds the folders of an added folder.
"Write a report of the run" leaves a text file beside the results saying what was written and what failed.
A PDF that is only signed keeps the signatures it has; if anything else is done to it in the same run, it is written anew and they are left out.

topics.title: The settings of PDF Organizer
body: File → Settings (or Settings on the side bar, then PDF Organizer). Each setting can be put back on its own, or all at once.

points: When a document opens: how large a document is shown when it opens, scrolling or one page at a time, thumbnails shown or not.
Units, rulers and grid: the unit (millimetres, inches, points), rulers, the grid and its spacing.
Printing: the paper, orientation and scaling the print window starts with.
Quick toolbar: which buttons the strip above the pages has.
Names of new documents: the patterns for extracted pages, new documents and the PDF that batch processing gathers many files in.
Signatures: whether "Save" asks before writing over a signed file.
Keyboard shortcuts: click the keys of a command, then press the new ones.

topics.title: About PDF Organizer
body: PDF Organizer is the PDF app of Syntelab Creative: it reads PDF documents, arranges and combines their pages, writes and draws on them, fills in and makes forms, signs with a certificate and checks signatures, and does the same things to many files at once.
It is new, and some of what it does is a first step. Where it falls short for your documents, tell us through Help → Feedback: that is how we know what to work on.

topics.title: What PDF Organizer is built with

points: Reading, drawing and writing PDF: MuPDF.
Recognizing text (OCR): Tesseract, when it is installed on the computer.
Opening office documents: Word, Excel and PowerPoint, or LibreOffice, whichever is installed.
Saving a web page as a PDF: the browser installed on the computer.
Signing with a certificate: the certificate services of Windows; signatures are written the way the PAdES standard asks.

body: What it shares with the rest of the program is under "About Syntelab Creative".

topics.title: What PDF Organizer cannot do yet

points: Office documents are opened by the office suite on the computer; without Word, Excel, PowerPoint or LibreOffice they cannot be opened. A converter of our own is being worked on: see "What we are working on".
Recognizing text needs the Tesseract engine, installed apart.
The text of a document itself is changed one line at a time; paragraphs do not flow again.
Pictures printed in four inks (CMYK) cannot be picked up to be moved.
Validate tells whether a certificate is revoked today, not when it was revoked.
Signing with a certificate works on Windows for now; on Linux and macOS it will come in a later version.

topics.title: The editor
body: Scribe is an editor of plain text with its tools beside it. Each text has a tab; the text is in the middle, the panel of tools on its side, and a line of facts under it.

When Scribe is opened it first asks what you would like to do: count words, find and replace, remove duplicates, compare two texts, sort lines, reverse a text, write filler or random text. Each choice opens the text with the tool for it beside; "An empty text" opens the text alone, and the texts opened lately are listed under.

points: File → New text (Ctrl+N) starts an empty text.
File → Open (Ctrl+O) opens one or several files, each in its tab. Any file that holds text opens: .txt, .md, .csv, .log, .srt, source code and others.
Edit → Undo (Ctrl+Z) and Redo (Ctrl+Y) go through everything done to the text, a tool or a recipe counting as one step.
Edit → Find and replace (Ctrl+F) opens a strip in the editor that goes from one match to the next.
Edit → Select all (Ctrl+A).

body: The line under the text shows where the cursor is, how much is selected, the number of lines, words and characters, the encoding of the file and how its lines end.

Files dropped on the window open too, each as a new text with the file's name, encoding and line endings. The program gets what is in a dropped file but not where it is on disk, so saving asks where; files over 64 MB are opened with File → Open.
A new text, while it is empty, lists the texts opened lately: click one to open it. "Forget the list" empties it; the list is kept on this computer only.

topics.title: Save and Save as
body: Nothing changes the file on disk until you save. A dot on the tab says the text has changes that are not in its file, and closing such a tab asks first.

points: Save (Ctrl+S) writes the text over its file. A new text asks where.
Save as (Ctrl+Shift+S) writes it to a new file, which then takes the tab's place, with everything that can be undone still there; the old file stays as it was.

body: A file is written whole or not at all: if writing fails, the file that was there is still there.

body.note: A file is saved the way it was opened: in the same encoding, with the same line endings. A text typed on Windows and one typed on Linux both stay what they were.

topics.title: Encodings and line endings
body: An encoding is the way letters are kept as bytes. Scribe reads what the file says about itself, and guesses when it says nothing. Most files today are UTF-8; older ones from Central Europe are often windows-1250.

points: Letters that look wrong (Ã£ in place of ă, or squares): File → "Read again in another encoding", and choose the one the file was written in.
To save in another encoding, choose it on the line under the text, then save. If the text has letters that encoding cannot write, Scribe says which and writes nothing.
Line endings (Windows CRLF, Linux and macOS LF, old Mac CR) are changed in the same place. A file with mixed endings is said to have them; saving gives all its lines the same.

body: What a new text starts with is chosen in Settings.

points: Everything in the View menu is a switch: on, it is seen; off, it is not.
Text: Wrap long lines (Alt+Z) — a line longer than the window goes on below, and the text keeps its lines; Line numbers; Result beside the text.
Beside the text: Tools (Ctrl+T), Recipes, Statistics. The panel shows only the parts that are on; with none on, there is no panel.

Tools shown: each group of tools (find and replace, lines, capitals and letters, cleaning, write text) can be left out of the panel. A tool chosen from the Format or the Tools menu is shown all the same: its part and its group come back by themselves.
The double arrow at the top of the panel folds it down to a strip at the edge, from which each of its parts is a click away; drag its edge to make it wider or narrower.
The letters and their size are chosen in Settings.

topics.title: Very large files
body: A file over 64 MB is not put in the editor: it opens in a tab that shows it a page of 500 lines at a time, read from the file as you go. Files of gigabytes open this way in the time it takes to go through them once.

points: "Previous page" and "Next page" move through it; a line number and "Go" jump to any line.
Find looks through the whole file, with the same choices as elsewhere, and lists the places it found: click one to go to its line. A long list comes a part at a time, with "Find more".
"Run a recipe on the whole file" writes the result into a folder you choose, under the same name. The file itself is never changed here.
"Open whole in the editor" puts it in the editor all the same, to change it by hand. It may be slow, and it needs several times the size of the file in memory.

body.note: Files written two bytes to a letter (UTF-16) cannot be shown a page at a time. A recipe holds the whole file in memory while it runs: the limit is the memory of the computer.

topics.title: How tools work
body: The tools are in the panel beside the text, in groups. Click a tool to see its choices, then Apply.

points: With something selected, a tool changes only the selection; with nothing selected, the whole text. The panel says which, at its top.
Under the button, a tool says what it did: how many lines or places it changed.
Every tool is one step: Undo takes it back whole.

Every tool is also in the menus and in the search of commands: those that change the shape of a text (lines, capitals and letters, cleaning) in the Format menu, the others in Tools. Choosing one there opens the panel at its choices.

body: In the Format menu, a tool that is mostly one choice is laid out as its options: every way to change capitals, every kind of quotation mark, every way to turn a text around is a command of its own, which opens the tool with that option chosen. Where the window is too narrow for a group, the group becomes one button that opens the whole list.
The tools run on this computer. No text leaves it.

topics.title: The result, before you apply
body: While a tool is open, what it would give is shown beside the text, in the "Result" pane. Nothing in the text changes until you choose Apply. The result follows you: change a choice or the text, and it is made again.

points: The text and the result stand side by side, each under a head of the same height, so the same lines start at the same height; they scroll together (the chain button turns that off).

Lines that would change are marked, with the part of the line that changes marked darker; lines that would only move, and lines that are new, each have their own colour. The lines that would be changed or taken out are marked in your text too.
Under the names: what would happen in numbers — lines changed, moved, new, taken out; lines and characters before and after.
Under the result: the lines that would be taken out. Click one to go to it in the text.

The small buttons of the result: copy it, open it as a new text, compare it with the text in a tab, scroll together, put the result under the text instead of beside it, hide it. The text has its own: undo, redo, copy, paste over, select all, clear.
Drag the bar between the two to give one more room; a double click makes them equal again.

body: After Apply, the Result pane says so ("Applied. The text on the left is now the result.") and offers Undo and "Compare with what it was", which opens the same comparison of before and after. It shows a result again as soon as you change the text or a choice of the tool.

body.note: View → "Result beside the text" turns the pane off and on. For a very long text (over two million characters) nothing is shown beforehand: apply the tool, and Undo takes it back.

topics.title: Replace everywhere
body: Replaces every place something is found, at once. While you type what to find, Scribe says in how many places it is found and marks them in the text, so you see what will change before you apply.

points: "Regular expression": the text to find is a pattern. In "Replace with", $1, $2… stand for what the groups of the pattern found.
"Capitals count": a and A are different letters.
"Whole words only": "cat" is not found inside "category".
"Keep the capitals of what is replaced": replacing "cat" with "dog" turns "Cat" into "Dog" and "CAT" into "DOG".

"More choices" → "Fill in…": what is put in place may hold blanks filled in at each match. {counter} counts 1, 2, 3… ({counter:10} starts at 10, {counter:10:5} goes up by 5); {date} and {time} are the day and the hour of your computer; {uuid} is an identifier; {random} is 8 random letters and digits ({random:12} for 12).
Under what you look for, Scribe also says on how many lines the matches are and how many different texts they are.

body: "Replace several at once" does a list of pairs in one step. Write one pair to a line, as: what to find => what to put in its place. They are done from the first to the last, each on what the one before left; an empty second half takes the text out.

body.note: A pattern cannot freeze the program: the time it takes grows with the length of the text and no faster. Patterns that look back at what they found (\1) are not available for that reason.

points: Sort lines by: their letters, as a dictionary does, in the language of the program or one you choose (in Romanian ă comes after a; Swedish puts ä after z, German beside a); letters with numbers as numbers (file2 before file10); the number each line starts with; length; number of words; the date each line starts with (05.03.2024, 2024-03-05, with or without an hour); internet addresses; version numbers (1.2.10 after 1.2.9); titles, where an article at the start does not count; an order you write (small, medium, large); or no order at all.
Lines with nothing to be sorted by (no number, no date, a value that is not in the order you wrote) stay at the end whichever way the others are sorted: smallest first or largest first.

More choices for sorting: compare from a word or a character on, or one column of a table (with what parts the columns); keep the first line in place as a heading; sort paragraphs instead of lines; and tidy first — trim, take out empty lines, take out duplicates.

Remove duplicate lines: keep the first, the last, or none of the lines that repeat (only those that are there once stay). Capitals, the spaces around a line, digits, punctuation, and a number of characters at the start or the end can each be passed over; only a column, or only what a pattern finds, can be what is compared. Empty lines are treated as the others, kept, taken out, or collapsed.
Count repeated lines: leaves each line once, with how many times it was there written before it — the most repeated first, or the least, or in the order they come.
Keep or drop lines: looks for something in every line and keeps only the lines that have it, or only those that do not.
Reverse the order of lines; Shuffle lines.
Number lines: the first number, what stands after it, zeros in front so the numbers line up, empty lines without a number.
Empty lines: remove them all, or leave one where there are several.

Join lines into one, with what you choose between them; Split into lines at every comma, semicolon or anything else. Wherever what stands between things is typed (numbering, joining, splitting, counting), \t stands for a tab, which cannot be typed into a field.

body.note: A choice that only matters with another is shown only then: the column, once you compare by a column. The choices fewer people need are under "More choices".

topics.title: Capitals
body: Change capitals: sentence case, every word with a capital, all capitals, all small letters, inverted, and the ways names are written in code: camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, CONSTANT_CASE, kebab-case.
Capitals follow the rules of each alphabet, not only of English.

In the Direction group, "Turn the text around" turns the letters of every line around, or the order of its words, or the letters of each word; "Upside down" writes it to be read from across the table, and "As in a mirror" also swaps the marks that have a left and a right. Letters are counted as a reader counts them: a letter with its marks stays one.

points: Clean up spaces: several spaces become one; spaces at the ends of lines go.
Trim line ends: at both ends, at the start or at the end.
Quotation marks: straight, English, Romanian, German or French.
Remove diacritics: ă becomes a, é becomes e. Only in the Latin and Greek alphabets, where a letter without its mark is still the letter.
Repair Romanian letters: ş and ţ (with a cedilla, written by older keyboards) become ș and ț (with a comma), the letters Romanian is written with.
Tabs to spaces and spaces to tabs, with the width of a tab you choose.

Remove HTML tags: for the source of a web page pasted into the text. The tags, scripts and styles go; what a reader would see stays. To bring a page from its address, use the tool under it, "Text of a web page".

Text of a web page: type the address of a page (example.com/page) and choose "Bring the text". What a reader would see on that page is written where the cursor is, without tags, scripts or styles. This is the one tool of Scribe that goes online, and only when you ask: the page is fetched by the browser installed on this computer (Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome), run without a window and without your cookies or sign-ins; the program itself sends nothing. A page that needs you to be signed in gives only what a stranger would see.

topics.title: Putting Romanian diacritics back
body: Romanian typed without ă, â, î, ș, ț is written with them again.

steps: Open the tool in the Cleaning group and choose Apply.
Words that have one right form are changed at once: "stiu" becomes "știu", "informatii" becomes "informații".
Words that can be read in more than one way (fata, fată, fața, față) are listed under the button, each in its place in the text. Click the right form for each.
Or tick "Choose the likelier form by itself" before applying: nothing is asked, and the result is to be read through.

body: Where the words around are enough, Scribe decides by them: "o casa" becomes "o casă", "casa mea" stays, "pentru ca" becomes "pentru că".

body.note: This is built for Scribe from a list of common words and the endings Romanian always writes with diacritics. Words it does not know (rare words, names) stay as they are typed, and a word already written with diacritics is never touched. Read the result before sending it.

topics.title: Writing text: filler and random
body: The tools of the "Write text" group change nothing: they write. What they give goes where the cursor is, in place of the selection.

points: Filler text: paragraphs, sentences, words, lists, headings, or parts of a page (a heading, paragraphs, a list). In printers' Latin (lorem ipsum), English, Romanian, the words of offices or of the kitchen, or your own words. More choices: short, medium or long sentences; plain text, Markdown, HTML or JSON; the level of the headings; a limit in characters (the text is cut at a whole word and still ends as a sentence); words to leave out.

Made-up data: names, e-mail addresses, phone numbers, street addresses, dates or numbers, one to a line, of Romania or of English-speaking countries. "Lines after my pattern" writes each line as you say, with {name}, {first}, {last}, {email}, {phone}, {address}, {street}, {city}, {date}, {number:1-100}, {word}, {letter}, {digit}, {uuid} and {row} standing for what is made — a table to try something on, in a moment.

Random text: passwords (letters, digits and marks, at least one of each), letters, digits, hexadecimal or identifiers (UUID), on one line or on many. Characters easily confused (0 and O, 1, l and I) can be left out.
A seed (under "More choices") makes filler and made-up data come out the same every time for the same number; 0 gives something new each time.

body.note: Passwords are made on this computer, from the randomness of the operating system, and are sent nowhere. Made-up e-mail addresses end in example.com, where mail reaches no one; a phone number made at random may be someone's, so do not call it.

topics.title: Keeping what you did as a recipe
body: A recipe is a list of tools with their choices, kept under a name and run again with one click.

steps: Apply to a text the tools you want, in the order you want them.
Open "Recipes" at the top of the panel: the tools you applied are listed.
"Keep as a recipe", and give it a name.
Later, open the recipe and choose "Run on the text": all its steps are done, and one Undo takes them all back.

body: Recipes are kept on this computer and are there in every text.

topics.title: Changing a recipe, or making one from nothing
body: "Change" on an open recipe shows its name and its steps. Each step can be moved up or down, taken out, and given other choices; tools are added from the list under the steps. Nothing is kept until "Save".
"New recipe" starts one with no steps, to be put together the same way without applying the tools to a text first.

body.note: The tools that write text (filler, random) are not steps of a recipe: a recipe changes a text.

topics.title: Running a recipe on files

steps: Open the recipe and, under "Run on files", add files or a folder (with the folders under it).
Choose where the results go: into another folder, which leaves the files as they are, or over the files themselves.
Run. Scribe says how many files were written, how many needed no change, and which could not be done and why.

body: Each file is written in the encoding and with the line endings it had. In another folder, files keep the folders they came with, and a file that is already there is never written over.

body.note: Writing over the files themselves cannot be undone from Scribe. Keep a copy if they matter.

topics.title: Statistics
body: "Statistics" at the top of the panel says what the text, or the selection, is made of. Each part folds away.

points: At the top: words, characters with and without spaces, sentences, paragraphs, lines, pages, and the size in bytes.
Time: to read in silence, to say aloud, to type, and to write by hand.
Words: how many are different (and what share of all), letters in a word, syllables, the longest and the shortest word, and how many words there are of each length.
Sentences: words in a sentence, how many are short, medium and long, how many are statements, questions and exclamations, and the longest and the shortest.

Ease of reading: a score from 0 (very hard) to 100 (very easy), by the formula made for the language of the text. Formulas exist for English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese and Russian; a language without one gets no score, since a formula made for another would mislead.
What it says most: the words used most with their share of the text, and the pairs and groups of three words that come back.
Room in the usual limits: how many characters are left, or over, for a title, a description, a short post and others.

body: Words and sentences are found by the rules of each script, so Chinese, Japanese and Thai, which put no spaces between words, are counted too. The speeds the times are reckoned with, and how many words make a page, are set in Settings.

topics.title: Comparing two texts

points: Tools → "Compare with another text": the text in the editor beside one you type or paste.
Tools → "Compare with a file": the text in the editor, as it is now, beside a file you choose.
Tools → "Compare two texts": two texts typed or pasted side by side.
Tools → "Compare two files".

body: The two texts are shown side by side. Lines only in the first are marked as removed, lines only in the second as added, and in a line that changed, the words that differ are marked. Only what differs is shown, with a few lines around; the arrows go from one difference to the next.

Capitals, spaces, empty lines, numbers and punctuation can each be passed over. "In one column" shows what was taken out above what was put in, each with its sign, instead of side by side. Beside the counts, Scribe says how alike the two texts are, as the share of lines that are the same.

A text is shown as soon as it is chosen, before the other is. Drag the bar between the two texts to give one more room; while the texts are typed, the bar under the boxes is dragged up and down to give the boxes or the comparison more room. A double click puts a bar back.
Where several lines in a row were changed, each is put beside the line it is most like, so a line added or taken out among them does not make every line after it look changed into the next.
"Type or paste the texts" shows a box over each column; what you write there is compared as you write, and a file can still be chosen for either side.

topics.title: Finding and replacing in a folder

steps: Tools → "Find in a folder" (Ctrl+Shift+F), and choose the folder. The folders under it are searched too.
Type what to find, with the same choices as "Replace everywhere". "Kinds of files" keeps the search to some endings (txt, md, csv…).
Every match is shown in its line, file by file. Click a line to open the file there.
To replace: type the new text, untick the files to leave alone, and choose "Write the files".

body: Nothing is written until you ask, and only in the files left ticked. Each file is written in the encoding and with the line endings it had.

body.note: Hidden folders and those programs fill (.git, node_modules) are passed over unless you ask for them. Files that are not text are passed over always.

topics.title: The settings of Scribe
body: File → Settings opens the program's Settings at Scribe's part.

points: The editor: letters of one width or the program's own, their size, wrapping, line numbers, and whether the result of a tool is shown before it is applied.
A new text: how its lines end, and whether its file starts with a byte order mark.
Statistics: the speeds of reading, saying, typing and writing by hand, and how many words make a page.
The keys of Scribe's commands.

body: Each setting has a button that puts it back as the program ships it.

topics.title: About Scribe
body: Scribe is the text app of Syntelab Creative: an editor with its tools beside the text. It shows what a tool would do before it does it, cleans and reorders lists, finds and replaces in a text or in a whole folder, compares two texts, says what a text is made of, writes filler and made-up data, and keeps what you do often as recipes to run again.
Everything is done on this computer. There is no limit put on the size or the number of texts: the limits are the memory of the computer and what today's technology can do.
It is new. Where it falls short for your texts, tell us through Help → Feedback: that is how we know what to work on.

topics.title: What Scribe is built with

points: The editor: CodeMirror.
Reading and writing encodings: encoding_rs, with chardetng to guess the encoding of a file that does not say it.
Finding and replacing: the regex library of Rust, whose patterns cannot freeze the program.
Sorting as each language does, and finding words and sentences in every script: ICU4X, the Unicode library.
Comparing texts: the similar library.
Romanian diacritics: a list of words and rules written for Scribe.

body: What it shares with the rest of the program is under "About Syntelab Creative".

points: A very large file is read a page at a time and changed only through recipes; changing it by hand means opening it whole, which takes memory.
Putting Romanian diacritics back knows the common words; rare words and names stay as typed.
There is no spelling check.
Text is not taken out of PDF or office documents here; PDF Organizer opens those.
The editor does not colour code or Markdown.
A file dropped on the window opens as a new text: the program is not told where the file is, so saving asks where.

topics.title: The converters
body: Units converts values between units of measure: one value quickly, or whole tables of values at once. Everything is computed on your computer.
The converters are in six menus: Essentials, Motion and mechanics, Energy and power, Scientific, Digital and media, and Specialized physics. Choosing one opens its table.

points: A converter opens in the tab you are in. If its table has values, you are asked first: Continue (the values are lost), Open in a new tab, or Cancel.
Settings → Units → "Open each converter in a tab of its own" opens every converter you choose in a new tab instead.
File → Go to Start goes back to the first page of Units.

topics.title: Quick convert
body: The first page of Units, Quick convert, converts one value from a unit to another. Choose a converter, type the value on the "From" side, and choose the two units: the result is on the "To" side.

points: Each side lists the popular units of the converter and your own units, with a search over them. The table of the converter has every unit.
The button between the two sides swaps the two units.
The bookmark beside a unit pins it: pinned units come first in both lists and in the units panel of the table.
The button in the result copies it; the × clears the value.
"Open in the table" opens the table of the converter.

topics.title: How numbers are read and written
body: You can type and paste numbers as they are written in different countries: 1,234.56 and 1.234,56 are both understood, as are spaces and apostrophes between thousands, and 1.5e-3 for a power of ten.
A number that can be read two ways (1,234: a thousand, or one and a bit) is read as the language of the program writes numbers, and the line under the table says so.

A result is written with the decimals of the unit it arrives in, not with as many digits as you typed: 5 cm is 1.97 in. A value that is not zero always shows a few digits that say something, so 1 cm is 0.00001 km and never 0.000 km.
Values too large or too small to read at a glance are written with a power of ten, as 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵. View → Extreme values in full writes them with every zero instead.
Where a unit has no such value (a sound pressure of zero has no decibels) the cell shows a dash.

topics.title: Rows and columns
body: Every column is a unit and every row a value. The cell you type in drives its row: the other columns show the same value in their units. The typed cell is shown in bold.
What is not a number is kept and shown in red; its row converts nothing until you put it right.

points: Double-click a cell, or just start typing on it, to edit. Enter moves down, Tab to the right; the arrow keys move; Escape leaves the cell as it was.
Click the corner (#) to select the whole table, a row number to select its row, a title to select its column. Shift+click selects a range, Ctrl+click adds cells, dragging selects too.

Home and End go to the first and the last column of the row; Ctrl+Home to the first cell of the table, Ctrl+End to the last. Ctrl with an arrow goes to the edge of the table: the first or last row, the first or last column. Page Up and Page Down move by a screen. With Shift, each of these stretches the selection instead.
A selection of several cells is outlined on its outside; the cell typing goes to stays unshaded inside it.
Delete empties the selected rows.
Typing in the last row adds a row. A table has no most it holds: it is as long as the memory of your computer allows (a row takes 16 bytes, so 100 million rows take about 1.5 GB).

topics.title: Columns and the units panel
body: The panel beside the table lists the units of the converter. At its top are the units in the table: click one to take its column out. Under them, every unit: search by name or symbol, filter by group or by "Popular", and click a unit to add it as a column.
The bookmark beside a unit pins it as a favourite: it comes first in the list and is first in Quick convert.

points: Columns share the width of the table equally until their titles no longer fit; then the table scrolls sideways.
Drag the edge of a title to change the width of its column; double-click the edge to fit the column to its longest value. The column of row numbers can be dragged too.
The ⋮ button of a column: move it left or right, pin it to the left or right edge, change its precision, or remove it.
The precision of a column changes that column only. "Use for this unit everywhere" makes it the precision of the unit, in every table and in Quick convert.
The button with two arrows beside Undo and Redo fits the columns to the table: every width you dragged or fitted goes, and the columns share the width of the table again.
The two upper parts of the panel, the units in the table and "Add units" (the search and the filters), fold away with a click on their names, so the list has more room.

topics.title: Undo, copy, paste, import and export
body: The bar over the table holds its tools.

points: Undo and Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y) go through every change of the table. A paste or an import is one step.
Copy (Ctrl+C) copies the whole table or what is selected, as a spreadsheet reads it. "Transposed" turns rows into columns.
Paste (Ctrl+V) puts copied rows into the table from the active cell down. If the first row holds titles of units, the columns are matched by them, and units that are not in the table yet are added.
Import reads an Excel workbook, a CSV or a TSV file in the place of what the table holds. "Find the format by itself" tells the kind by the file.

Export writes the table as Excel, CSV, TSV or JSON. With a comma before the decimals, CSV is written with semicolons, as spreadsheets expect. A sheet of Excel holds 1,048,576 rows: a longer table goes on on the next sheets of the same workbook, under the same titles.
The eraser empties the selected rows; the bin empties the whole table.

body: A row holds one value. Of a pasted or imported row that has several values, the first is taken and the others are computed from it.

Very many rows take a while to paste, import, export or copy. A card over the table then shows how far the work has got, in percent and in rows, with a Stop button. A paste or an import that is stopped leaves the table as it was; an export that is stopped writes no file.

When the computer has no memory left for the rows, nothing is changed and the line under the table says how much was needed. When the rows fit but the table as it was could not be kept beside them, you are asked whether to continue without undo: that change, and those before it, can then no longer be taken back. Before asking, the oldest steps of Undo are let go to make room.

Table options (the gear): what the title of a column says (name and symbol, name, or symbol), whether copies and exports include the titles and the row numbers, "Start this converter with these columns", and "Reset the table".

topics.title: Currency
body: Currencies have no fixed factor: what one is worth changes. The currency converter reads its rates from two free services while you use it, and only then.

points: Currencies of countries: Rates By Exchange Rate API, https://www.exchangerate-api.com . They change once a day at their source, and are read no more often than that.

Cryptocurrencies: Powered by CoinGecko, https://www.coingecko.com . They are read when the converter is opened or comes back to the front and what it has is older than a quarter of an hour, and when you press Refresh; never on a timer.

body: Only the rates are asked for. Nothing about you is sent, and never the amounts you convert.

The line under the table, and under the result of Quick convert, says when the rates are of. Without a connection the last rates are used and marked as old. A currency the services give no rate for shows a dash.

Settings → Units → Currency: "Read the rates from the network" can be turned off, and the converter then uses the last rates it kept. "Name the sources beside the rates" shows or hides the names of the two services on that line.
The rates are for information. Do not rely on them for a transaction.

topics.title: Number base
body: The units of this converter are ways of writing a whole number: bases from 2 to 64, Roman numerals, base 60 with colons (1:30:15), binary-coded decimal and Gray code. Their values are text: type FF under hexadecimal and the other columns show 255, 11111111 and so on.
Roman numerals go from I to MMMCMXCIX (1 to 3999).

topics.title: Units that are not a plain factor
body: Most units are a factor of another. Some are not, and Units converts them as they are defined: temperatures with their offsets; fuel economy (litres per 100 km against miles per gallon); a wavelength against a frequency; conductance against resistance; degrees Baumé, API, Brix and Plato against density; decibels against sound pressure and intensity; a slope in percent against its angle.

A temperature and a difference of temperature are not the same thing: 100 °C is 212 °F, but a difference of 100 °C is a difference of 180 °F. The units of the group "Difference (Δ)" convert among themselves; between them and the temperature scales a cell shows a dash.

topics.title: Making a unit
body: You can add units of your own to any converter. In the units panel, choose "New unit", give it a name and a symbol, and say it by a unit that exists.

points: A factor: "1 pace = 0.75 m". For a scale that does not start at zero, also what is added after multiplying.
A formula: how the value becomes the other unit, with x for the value, and the formula for the way back. For example x * 9 / 5 + 32 and (x - 32) * 5 / 9.

body: What you type is tried as you type it, and what one of your unit comes to is shown before you keep it. A formula can use + − × ÷ ^, brackets, x, pi, e, and the functions sqrt, abs, ln, log, log2, exp, sin, cos, tan, asin, acos and atan. It is worked out, never run as a program.
Your units are listed under "Mine" in the panel, where they can be changed and removed. A unit of yours can be said by another unit of yours; removing a unit removes those said by it.
Settings → Units lists your units of every converter, and exports and imports them as text you can keep or move to another computer.

topics.title: Settings of Units
body: File → Open Settings opens the settings of Units; so do the options of the table (the gear in its bar).

points: Open each converter in a tab of its own, or in the tab you are in.
Extreme values in full, what is written between thousands (10000.000, 10 000.000 or 10,000.000; nothing unless you choose otherwise), and row numbers.
Currency: whether the rates are read from the network, and whether the services are named beside them.

Precision of units: choose a converter (or "Units you changed"), search for a unit, and set its decimals with − and +; the arrow takes it back to the unit's own. "Use for this unit everywhere" in the menu of a column sets the same value.
Units a table starts with: the converters whose first columns you chose, each with a way back to those it ships with.
Your own units.

topics.title: About Units
body: Units is the converter app of Syntelab Creative: 38 converters with more than 1,500 units, from length and temperature to currencies and number bases. A value typed once is shown in every unit you ask for, in a table that takes one value or millions of them.

Numbers are worked out exactly, as fractions, and rounded only when they are written. Everything is done on this computer; only the rates of currencies are read from the network, and that can be turned off.
It is new. Where it falls short for your work, tell us through Help → Feedback: that is how we know what to work on.

topics.title: How many rows a table holds: what we measured
body: A table has no fixed limit of rows: it is as long as the memory of your computer allows. A row takes 16 bytes, so 100 million rows take about 1.5 GB. When the memory runs out, the table stays as it was and the program says how much was needed.
We measured it with 50,000,000 rows, each a number in one column, in the optimised build of the program:

points: Pasting 50,000,000 rows: about 7 seconds.
Importing them from a CSV file: 12 seconds.
Exporting them to a CSV file, with a second column converted: about 3.5 minutes.
Exporting them to Excel, on 48 sheets: 4.3 minutes.

body: Going out takes longer than coming in because every cell that is written is converted exactly first.

body.note: The computer the test ran on: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D (16 cores, 32 threads), 64 GB of memory, Windows 11 Pro. October 2026. On another computer the times will differ; the size of a row will not.

topics.title: What Units is built with

points: Exact numbers: the num libraries of Rust (fractions of whole numbers of any size).
The units, their factors and their groups: data files of the program, one for each converter.
Reading Excel and OpenDocument workbooks: calamine. Writing Excel workbooks: rust_xlsxwriter.
The clipboard of the system, for copies and pastes of very many rows: arboard.
The rates of currencies: ExchangeRate-API and CoinGecko (see "Currency").

body: What it shares with the rest of the program is under "About Syntelab Creative".

points: A row holds one value: of a pasted row with several values, the first is taken.
Exporting very many rows is slow (see what we measured).
What is copied to the clipboard is held in memory as one text before it is pasted.
The rates of currencies are as fresh as their two sources give them: once a day for the currencies of countries.
